content: Selenium deficiency has been identified as a potential factor in chronic asthma. Observational studies have shown that individuals with chronic asthma may have lower selenium levels compared to healthy controls. Despite this, selenium supplementation has not been routinely recommended as part of asthma treatment alongside standard drug therapy. This review systematically analyzed randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to evaluate the role of selenium supplementation in managing chronic asthma. The primary aim was to determine whether selenium supplementation, when used in addition to asthma medications, could reduce the symptoms and overall impact of chronic asthma. To gather relevant data, searches were conducted in the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register, MEDLINE/PubMed, and EMBASE databases, with the most recent search completed in August 2005. The inclusion criteria focused on RCTs that compared outcomes in patients with chronic asthma who received selenium supplementation alongside their asthma medications versus those who received only standard asthma medications. Only one trial met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 24 patients with chronic asthma. The results of this study indicated a significant clinical improvement in the group receiving selenium supplementation compared to the placebo group, based on a general 'clinical evaluation.' However, this improvement was not supported by significant changes in objective measures of lung function or airway hyper-responsiveness. The authors concluded that selenium supplementation might have potential as an adjunctive treatment for chronic asthma. However, this conclusion is limited by the small number of studies available and the lack of measurable improvements in objective clinical parameters of lung function. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and establish the role of selenium in asthma management.
